1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Callerby Construct is a regional general contractor. It built Corran Valley Medical Centre, a four-storey steel-frame medical building, for the developer Halden Medical Properties under a £14.6m contract. The contract completion date was 30 April 2026. Practical completion came on 29 October 2026. Halden is deducting liquidated damages. Callerby's project director and a claims consultant have drafted a claim that blames the delay on Halden. Halden blames Callerby. The project's lender appointed an independent monitoring surveyor, and the project ran its information requests (RFIs) through a shared platform hosted by a third party. Callerby's Northern region also delivered Kestrel, a distribution warehouse, over the same period.
9	Your request: Callerby's chief executive wants to know what actually caused the Corran Valley slip, and what Callerby should do about the drafted extension-of-time and prolongation claim, which is due to go to Halden on 1 December. She also wants to know what should happen inside the company.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from Ruth Abernethy, chief executive, Callerby Construct, 12 Nov 2026 (leadership-account): 'Corran Valley Medical Centre reached practical completion on 29 October, 26 weeks after the contract date of 30 April. Halden is withholding £1.17m in liquidated damages. Our extension-of-time and prolongation claim for £1.9m is due to go to Halden on 1 December. Gareth says the slip is down to Halden's design changes and their architect's slow answers; Halden says the opposite. Before I sign anything I need to know what actually drove the slip and what we do next. On a brighter note, the Northern region had a good year: Kestrel warehouse handed over seven weeks early in March, and the regional early-handover incentive paid out to Colm Faraday's team.'
12	- Interview notes, Gareth Imrie, project director, 4 Nov 2026 (manager-account): Says Halden 'redesigned the building while we were building it'. Cites six change orders, CO-07 to CO-12, including CO-09, which moved the MRI suite to level 2. Halden flagged it in September and it needed extra steel. 'We couldn't carry on with the frame until CO-09 was resolved, and the architect sat on our steel connection queries for weeks.' Confirms the tower crane went to the Kestrel job in October: 'Kestrel's hired crane failed its thorough examination, the region needed one, and ours was standing idle anyway. Colm and I agreed it.' Says he has 'had a word' with the site superintendent about 'chatting to Halden's clerk of works'.
13	- Draft claim summary, Fenmore Claims Advisory, prepared for Callerby, 28 Oct 2026 (document): The time impact analysis attributes the full 26-week delay to employer risk events: (a) owner change orders CO-07 to CO-12, issued 12 Sep–9 Dec 2025 and holding the structural frame: 17 weeks; (b) late information: 41 of 64 RFIs, including structural connection queries, open longer than the contractual response period: a further 9 weeks. RFI durations come from the 'created' date in the project RFI log. Programme inputs are the contractor's monthly updates. Claimed: a 26-week extension of time and £1.9m in prolongation costs. Engagement terms: Fenmore's fee includes 6% of sums recovered.
14	- Letter, Priya Varma, development manager, Halden Medical Properties, to Callerby, 10 Nov 2026 (customer-account): 'We understand a delay claim is being prepared, so please note our position now. Your tower crane left site in October 2025 and did not come back until April. Your own superintendent told our clerk of works it had gone to another of your jobs. Our architect answered your queries promptly. The change orders concerned interior layouts and were small.' Halden will deduct liquidated damages in full and reserves its right to recover its own extra consultant and finance costs from Callerby.
15	- Interview notes, Dale Pruitt, site superintendent, 5 Nov 2026 (staff-account): 'Autumn and winter were dead. The crane and the frame gang went over to Kestrel and we did bits: drainage, level 1 blockwork.' Asked why: 'Above my pay grade. Gareth and Colm sorted it.' Asked whether levels 3–4 could have gone up: 'Steel was on the ground. Whether every connection query was answered, I couldn't swear to; that's Gareth's side.' Recalls that steel deliveries for levels 1–2 were 'all over the place in the summer'. Confirms he told Halden's clerk of works where the crane had gone: 'He asked. I wasn't going to lie.'
16	- Callerby monthly progress report no. 14 to Halden, November 2025, signed G. Imrie (document): 'Frame: level 3–4 erection resequenced pending resolution of CO-09 structural information and outstanding connection queries. Tower crane temporarily demobilised to reduce standing costs during the design hold.' The programme update moves frame completion from 19 Dec 2025 to 'TBC – subject to CO-09'. Stated critical path: CO-09 design → frame → envelope → fit-out. The report does not yet claim any change to the contract completion date.
17	
18	BRIEF:
19	The evidence does not support the claim as drafted. The platform's audit trail, which users can't edit, shows the architect answered 62 of 64 queries within the contract period. The "late" queries in the claim were measured from when Callerby opened its own drafts, and 39 of the 41 sat in Callerby's drafts for 9–47 days. The structural query on CO-09 was answered in four days. Meanwhile the tower crane left in October 2025 and came back in April 2026. It went to the Kestrel job, and the site diaries record the frame as "on hold – design" throughout. Gareth's own report described the crane's removal as cost-saving. So Callerby's redeployment of the crane is the best-supported cause. Whether the change orders, especially CO-09, cost any time is still unknown. Do not submit the claim as drafted on 1 December, since it would rest on a misleading measure. Do not discipline the superintendent, who answered honestly. Do not suspend the incentive scheme yet, because the link to the crane move is unproven. Next, commission an independent delay analysis, with a fee not tied to the amount recovered. It should test CO-09's real effect and Callerby's own share of the delay. Then decide whether to submit a narrower claim or settle. I'm moderately confident in this, not fully.
20
